blocks.heading: Platform By Platform
rows: YouTube long-form ads

No official figure. Your own revenue per 1,000 views (RPM) is shown in YouTube Studio once you are in the Partner Programme. Public estimates for India differ widely by niche and by where your viewers live.
Illustrative maths only: at an RPM of ₹100, 100,000 views in a month is about ₹10,000. Use your own RPM, not someone else's.
YouTube Shorts
Usually far lower per view than long-form. Check the separate Shorts RPM in your own analytics.
Shorts build an audience; they rarely pay the bills by themselves.
Brand deals and sponsorships
Nano creators with a clear niche can land paid posts in the low thousands; rates rise with engagement and proof of results
Closer to freelance client work than passive income. You need a pitch, a media kit and an invoice.
Affiliate links, your own products, memberships and services
No single figure; income depends on audience trust and what you sell
This is the layer that scales, because you own the offer and the customer relationship.

figures.label: Pay Range
figures.source: In India, 1 lakh views typically earns somewhere between ₹1,500 and ₹5,000, with finance, education, and business content usually paying a higher CPM than entertainment.

figures.label: Market Size
figures.source: To even qualify for YouTube's Partner Program you need 1,000 subscribers and 4,000 valid public watch hours in the last 12 months, or 10 million Shorts views in 90 days.

blocks.heading: Brand Deals and Building a Media Kit

items.text: Quote a package, not just a post.
Anchor on engagement rate, not just follower count.
Price the deal on what it's worth to the brand, not on your own cost or effort.
Ask for usage rights and exclusivity separately.
Get terms in writing before you post.

blocks.heading: Mistakes That Keep Creator Income Stuck

items.text: Chasing follower count instead of a defined niche.
Waiting for ad revenue to become the main income.
No owned audience outside the platform.
Underpricing brand deals and products out of fear of losing the deal.
Treating a good month as the new normal.
